title: The Blindness of China’s All-Seeing State
gist: Only a teaser is available: Wang argues China's pervasive surveillance teaches citizens to perform loyalty while hiding beliefs, so repression distorts the very information the Party needs to understand society.

insights.claim: China's relentless surveillance has taught people to perform obedience and loyalty while keeping their beliefs hidden.
insights.speaker: YAQIU WANG
insights.so_what: Official data and public sentiment signals from China may be systematically unreliable.
insights.quote: repression distorts the very information the government needs to understand society

insights.claim: Repression creates a dilemma for the Communist Party because it distorts the information the government needs to understand society.
insights.speaker: YAQIU WANG
insights.so_what: Raises policy-error and stability risk from information distortion.

insights.claim: At a garden in Yangzhou, visitors must scan their faces to receive toilet paper and the dispenser refuses a second serving.
insights.speaker: YAQIU WANG
insights.so_what: Illustrates how deeply facial recognition penetrates routine life.

insights.claim: In Shenzhen, police use facial recognition to catch jaywalkers, send penalties to their phones and notify their employers.
insights.speaker: YAQIU WANG
insights.so_what: Shows linkage of surveillance to social and employment sanctions.

insights.claim: For China-registered users, WeChat messages and images are automatically screened, and police monitored one human-rights lawyer's exchanges before detaining him.
insights.speaker: YAQIU WANG
insights.so_what: Domestic platforms act as surveillance infrastructure.
